value.overview: The Sungrebe, also called the American Finfoot, is a secretive tropical waterbird adapted to quiet freshwater habitats. It swims using lobed toes, often keeping its long tail spread across the water. Its reddish-brown body, boldly marked black-and-white head, and yellow-and-black legs help distinguish it from rails, grebes, and kingfishers. The species is unusual among birds because the male carries newly hatched chicks in specialized pouches beneath his wings.
value.classification: The Sungrebe is Heliornis fulica, the only living species in the genus Heliornis. It belongs to the finfoot family Heliornithidae within the order Gruiformes.
value.identification: This medium-small waterbird measures about 27 to 30 centimeters long. It has a dark crown and nape, a white throat, pale stripes along the sides of the neck, and mostly rich reddish-brown upperparts and body plumage. The long tail is conspicuous when the bird swims or flies. Its legs are boldly banded yellow and black, and its toes are broadly lobed. Females are generally brighter, with orange-rufous cheek patches and a more vivid eye ring during breeding.
value.rangeHabitat: The Sungrebe occurs from northeastern Mexico through Central America and into northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a local resident, mainly associated with lowland waterways on the Caribbean slope, including the Tortuguero region, Río Frío, Caño Negro, and other slow-flowing rivers and canals. It also occurs locally in the Osa Peninsula and Golfo Dulce area on the southern Pacific slope. Preferred sites have dense overhanging vegetation, muddy or gently flowing water, aquatic plants, fallen branches, and secluded banks, generally at low elevations.
value.migrationStatus: The Sungrebe is considered nonmigratory and resident throughout its range. In Costa Rica, it is expected year-round in suitable lowland wetlands and forested waterways rather than occurring as a seasonal migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding is associated with the wet season and higher water levels. Pairs build a loose platform nest from twigs, reeds, and leaves, usually close to or about a meter above the water in low vegetation. Both adults participate in incubation. After hatching, the male carries the young in specialized feather-lined pouches beneath his wings until they are able to swim and feed independently. This distinctive parental behavior is one of the species' best-known biological features.
value.dietFeeding: The Sungrebe forages quietly along vegetated stream margins and among floating or emergent plants. Its diet is thought to include aquatic insects, other small invertebrates, small fish, amphibians, and some plant material. It may pick prey from the water surface or vegetation, and it can swim and dive when disturbed or while pursuing food. Dense cover is important because the species usually feeds away from exposed shorelines and open water.
value.behavior: This is a shy, elusive bird that spends much of its time swimming slowly through shaded waterways or moving through dense marginal vegetation. It often freezes, slips into cover, or submerges when approached. Sungrebes defend territories and communicate with descending hoots, softer calls, and sharper notes during alarm. Pairs may call to one another during courtship and nesting. The species is usually solitary or found in pairs, and it avoids heavily disturbed watersides.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not well quantified. Sungrebes are difficult to survey because they are secretive and occur at low density in dense wetland vegetation, so local declines or changes may go undetected.
